opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think a lot of it comes down to timing and luck. When I started working on linear attention and efficient sequence modeling, it wasn't a very popular direction. Most people believed the Transformer had basically won and that alternatives like RNNs were a thing of the past. So there was a lot of open space. You didn't have to compete with hundreds of groups on the same idea.

Then, quite quickly, the field started caring a lot about long context and inference efficiency, and models like Mamba drew attention to this whole area. Suddenly the problems I'd been thinking about became very relevant. So part of it is that I happened to be standing in the right place when the wind changed.

But I'd also say it's about choosing the right kind of problem. I've always cared about the intersection of algorithms and hardware. A lot of earlier work on linear attention looked good in theory, but it wasn't actually fast on GPUs, so nobody used it. I spent a lot of time on the unglamorous parts, like writing efficient kernels and figuring out how to make chunkwise parallel training work well. That's also why we built the flash-linear-attention library. Once there's a fast, easy-to-use implementation, other people can build on your work, and that creates a positive feedback loop. People try your methods, give feedback, and new ideas come out of that.

And of course I've been fortunate with collaborators and advisors who gave me a lot of freedom. I could follow my own taste instead of chasing whatever was hot. I think having that freedom, plus being stubborn about a direction I believed in, made a big difference.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think "smooth" is quite the right word, because it felt like a lot of trial and error from the inside. But if I had to point to things that helped, I'd say a few.

The first is that I picked a problem early and stuck with it. I started working on linear attention and efficient sequence modeling before it was popular, when most people thought Transformers had basically settled the question. That meant the space was less crowded, and I could build up a lot of context on one line of work instead of jumping around. When the field started paying attention to things like Mamba and linear RNNs again, I already had a lot of the groundwork done.

The second is that I cared about the engineering side, not just the algorithmic side. A lot of ideas in this area look good on paper but die because nobody can make them run fast on a GPU. So I spent a lot of time writing Triton kernels, and that eventually became the flash-linear-attention library. Having a shared codebase where I could test ideas quickly made the research loop much faster, and it also meant other people started using it, which brought in collaborators and feedback.

The third is collaboration. My advisor Yoon Kim gave me a lot of freedom, and I worked closely with people like Yu Zhang and others who were just as obsessed with these questions. A lot of the papers, like Gated Linear Attention and the DeltaNet work, came out of long conversations where we kept pushing on what was actually the bottleneck.

And the last part is just that I enjoyed it. I was genuinely curious whether you could get Transformer-level quality without the quadratic cost, and that curiosity carried me through the parts that didn't work.

astra-6.text: I’m not sure I’d call it smooth all the way through. A PhD can look quite straightforward when you hear the finished story, because the false starts and uncertainty tend to get left out. I think progress comes from finding a manageable question, being willing to revise your approach, and asking for help when you get stuck. It’s less about always knowing the next step and more about gradually figuring it out.

sol-6.1.text: I think it comes down to having good guidance, a supportive research environment, and a bit of luck. Research can look smooth from the outside, but there are usually plenty of failed attempts along the way. What helps is breaking a big question into smaller ones, discussing problems early, and being willing to change direction when something isn’t working.
